No. The implication fails. Here is a counterexample.

**Counterexample.** Take $\mathcal{A}=M_2(\mathbb{C})$ with the usual operator norm. Set
$$
a=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Both $a$ and $b$ are orthogonal projections, hence positive ($a\geq 0$, $b\geq 0$), and $\|a\|=\|b\|=1$, so $\|a\|\leq\|b\|$ holds (in fact with equality).

Now compute
$$
b-a=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
This is self-adjoint with eigenvalues $-1$ and $1$. Since it has a negative eigenvalue, it is **not** positive. Therefore $a\nleq b$.

**Conclusion.** The condition $\|a\|\leq\|b\|$ for positive elements only controls the spectral radius (which for positive elements equals the norm), not the order relation. Positivity of $b-a$ requires $\sigma(b-a)\subseteq[0,\infty)$, a much stronger condition than a comparison of norms. Thus $\|a\|\leq\|b\|$ does **not** imply $a\leq b$.

### PROOF COMPLETE

But $b - a = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue $-1$, so not positive. Hence $a \not\leq b$.
